newsitem.title: INDIA: INSTANT VIEW-India RBI cuts interest rates.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-India RBI cuts interest rates.

text.p: Bankers and analysts reactions to the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) decision to cut interest rates by one percentage point on Wednesday:
R. NAGARAJAN, GENERAL MANAGER, BANK OF INDIA

"Banks have been talking about further cuts in lending rates. This will act as a catalyst. RBI wants to make the cost of borrowing cheaper. It is another way RBI is using the bank rate as a tool to play with interest rates."
K.C. CHAKRAVARTY, DEPUTY GENERAL MANAGER, BANK OF BARODA

"The RBI is signalling banks to move to a low-cost economy. Banks that cannot adapt will not be able to onlend. Long-term lending rates have to fall. Credit offtake depends on issues other than lending rate.
"Over the past one year, lending rates have fallen by 200 to 250 basis points but there has been no spurt in credit offtake."
RAMNATH IYER, STRATEGIST, PEREGRINE CAPITAL INDIA
"It is very positive for the markets. It was completely unexpected as there is already a lot of liquidity. It is a positive surprise in a market more used to negative ones."

Iyer said the cut the bank rate from 11 to 10 percent and deposits up to one year from nine to eight percent should provide banks with leeway to cut their prime lending rates. Currently the main state run Indian banks' PLRs are around 14.0-14.5 percent.
"They are likely to cut by 50 basis points. It may not happen tomorrow. They may mull it over but I think they'll do that (cut by 50 b.p.)."
KALPANA MORPARIA, GENERAL MANAGER, ICICI
"Money has been pouring into banks as investors in finance and other companies are shifting to banks. Instead of rolling over fixed deposits, they are depositing the money in banks.
"I think this (cut in interest rate on deposits) is a reaction to that."
S.R. KRISHNAN, ANALYST, PEREGRINE CAPITAL INDIA
"Without a deposit cut, banks cannot cut prime lending rates (PLR) (referring to RBI cutting interest rate on deposits of 30 days to one year to 8.0 percent from 9.0 percent).

"But the real question is whether interest rates are standing in the way of credit offtake. Despite a PLR at 14.0 percent and CP (commercial paper) at 9.0-10.0 percent, there is no real demand for credit. Banks' margins will be squeezed further."
S.SOLOMON RAJ, MANAGING DIRECTOR, INDUSIND BANK
"Indian interest rates are still high (the lowest lending rate is 14.0 percent per annum). It has to fall to at least 12.0 percent over a period of time.
"I think all banks will now cut lending rates - I see a cut of 0.5-1.0 percentage point cut (following RBI's decision to cut cap on one year deposit)."
RAMAMOORTHY GANESH, CEO, BIRLA CAPITAL AMC LTD
"A lot of money has been moving away from NBFCs (non-bank finance companies) to banks at a time when credit offtake has been poor. Banks could have got into a tight situation.
"The RBI move could help mutual funds as the return on mutual funds would not fall immediately as it would in the bond market."
SUBRA SUBRAMANIAM, DIRECTOR, HG ASIA
He said there were two main reasons why the central bank has cut interest rates.

The lower rates will help exporters by reducing the cost of their funding. Exporters are suffering due to the continued strength of the rupee against international currencies due to heavy foreign capital inflows.
Interest rate cuts would not undermine the rupee strength so long as the currency was not fully convertible on the capital account.
He said the central bank was also seeking to boost demand and provide the right environment for investment after the tax-cutting budget for 1997/98 passed in April.
"After all the good news of the budget the RBI is doing its part to get a broad revival going by pushing demand through interest rate cuts."

He said the RBI had leeway to cut its bank rate as inflation at just below six percentage points was around two percentage points below its year ago level, while the bank rate until today's announcement was just one percentage point lower than its year-ago level.
He said the government had resisted pressures to increase spending to get the economy moving, but through interest rates and tax cuts had sent a clear signal to the private sector to invest.
"The private sector must do its work."
